title: Ferran Torres' World Cup Mural Vandalised in Barcelona Amid Catalan Tensions
excerpt: Street artist TVBoy's tribute to Spain's World Cup hero was painted over with pro-Catalan independence slogans within 24 hours of its unveiling in Barcelona's Gràcia neighbourhood.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ferran Torres' mural was vandalized within 24 hours of its unveiling in Barcelona.
  • Graffiti included anti-Spain slogans and calls for Catalan independence.
  • Barcelona City Council cleaned and repainted the wall black after the vandalism.
  • The incident highlights ongoing tensions between Catalan identity and Spanish nationalism.
  • Torres' celebration wearing a 'Make Spain Great Again' hat intensified the backlash.
Catalonia's Tensions Erupt
›Mural unveiled in Gràcia neighbourhood
›Vandalized within 24 hours
›Graffiti included 'P*** Espanya' and pro-Catalan messages
›Barcelona City Council intervened to repaint the wall
Diario AS, Times of India

A mural celebrating Spain's 2026 World Cup hero Ferran Torres lasted less than a day in Barcelona before being defaced with pro-Catalan independence slogans. The vandalism has reignited debate over the fraught relationship between Catalan identity and Spanish nationalism in a city that has long been a flashpoint for both.

TVBoy's Tribute Sparks Immediate Backlash

The artwork was created by TVBoy, an Italian-born street artist based in Barcelona known for high-profile murals of footballers including Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, and Lamine Yamal. Painted in the city's Gràcia neighbourhood, the mural depicted Torres kissing the World Cup trophy alongside the words "Making history" and two stars representing Spain's two World Cup titles — 2010 and 2026.

https://x.com/sportstarweb/status/2079981342734045277

Torres had emerged as an unlikely hero in the final at MetLife Stadium in New York, coming off the bench in the 62nd minute and scoring the decisive goal in the 106th minute from a Nico Williams pass. Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in a match where La Roja dominated with 65 percent possession and 20 shots, while Argentina failed to register a single attempt on target, according to OneFootball.

The mural also arrived against the backdrop of Torres' post-final celebration, during which the 26-year-old Barcelona forward wore a hat reading "Make Spain Great Again" — a gesture that drew attention well beyond football circles, including a response from the White House.

Anti-Spain Graffiti and Catalan Independence Messages

Within hours of its unveiling, the mural was painted over multiple times, according to Diario AS. The first graffiti read "P*** Espanya," an anti-Spain expletive. That was subsequently replaced with "Espanya," before the wall was again overwritten — this time with the message "volem seleccions catalanes" ("we want Catalan national teams"), reflecting a longstanding demand from Catalan separatists for independent sports representation.

"A girl passed by and shouted: 'Mom, it's Ferran Torres!' I smiled. Then I understood that art also connects generations."

— TVBoy, street artist

TVBoy said the mural had already made its impact before the vandals arrived, recounting the moment a young girl recognized Torres while he was still painting. Barcelona City Council ultimately stepped in, cleaning the graffiti from the wall and repainting it black, according to the Times of India.

A City Where Sport, Art, and Politics Collide

The episode is not unprecedented in Barcelona. TVBoy's mural of Lamine Yamal, also in the Gràcia neighbourhood, was similarly vandalised last year following the teenager's 18th birthday celebration, though the artist later restored it. The pattern speaks to the unique political environment in Catalonia, where Spanish national symbols — even celebrations of sporting triumph — can trigger a visceral backlash from independence supporters.

The demand for separate Catalan national teams has been a recurring issue in Spanish politics. Catalonia has its own football federation, but its team is not recognized by FIFA or UEFA, a source of frustration for separatist movements that see sport as a vehicle for national identity. Torres' unambiguous embrace of Spain — culminating in the "Make Spain Great Again" hat — placed him at the centre of that divide.

What's Next

Despite lasting little more than a day, the mural sparked conversation beyond football, highlighting how sport, art, and politics often collide in Barcelona. TVBoy has a track record of restoring vandalised works — he repaired the Yamal mural after similar damage — but has not yet indicated whether he plans to recreate the Torres piece. For now, the blank black wall in Gràcia stands as its own kind of statement.
